$note: How a release is decided here: release-please reads the conventional commits since the last
tag, opens a pull request that bumps the version and writes RELEASES.md, and cutting the tag
is what MERGING that pull request does. The release workflow already in this repository is
include-component-in-tag is FALSE, deliberately and only here. This repository ships ONE
product, so a component prefix distinguishes it from nothing; its release workflow triggers on
`v*` and a prefixed tag would not start it at all — the release would silently produce nothing.
The sibling repositories carry prefixes because four products share one tag namespace there.
$exclude: A COMMIT THAT ONLY TOUCHES CI IS NOT A RELEASE, and this is the mechanism rather than the
reminder. From the action's own schema: "Path of commits to be excluded from parsing. If ALL
files from commit belong to one of the paths it will be skipped."
Why it is here: `feat(ci): release-please runs on main` — a change to nothing but a workflow —
duly proposed 0.3.0, a MINOR release of a product whose code had not moved. release-please reads
the type literally, and `feat` means a feature. It then happened twice more in the sibling
repositories on 2026-09-21, after the rule had been written down. A note that fails three times
is not a rule, it is a wish; this is configuration, and it cannot be forgotten.
THE TRADE, said out loud: a change to `.github` that genuinely alters the product — a compiler
flag, a build argument — is now skipped too. It rides along with the next real change, or its
author adds a `Release-As:` footer. That is the smaller of the two errors: the other one inflates
a version every single time anybody edits a workflow.
`ci:` and `chore:` remain the right types for such a commit regardless. This stops the mistake
from reaching a version number; it does not make the type meaningless.
